::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## In one sentence
I fossilize modern microbes in the lab, to help recognise them in ancient rocks and on other planets.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

## For everyone

Microbes were the only life on Earth for most of its history, and they are the most
likely kind of life we could find elsewhere in the Solar System. The problem: bacteria
are tiny, soft and easily destroyed. Over millions of years, heat and pressure in the
Earth's crust rework rocks, and most microbial traces disappear or end up looking like
ordinary minerals.

So I run the process forward, in the lab. I grow mats of bacteria that live on sulfur
and iron, let minerals form on and around them, and then put them in an autoclave that
simulates being buried deep underground. Afterwards, I check which shapes, minerals and
chemical fingerprints are still there.

The result is a field guide to what a fossil microbe *should* look like, useful both for
reading Earth's oldest rocks and for deciding which samples a Mars rover should bring home.

## For scientists

My research investigates how microbial biosignatures from sulfur- and iron-cycling
bacterial mats are fossilized through **experimental taphonomy under hydrothermal
conditions**. I combine geochemical, microbiological and mineralogical analyses to
understand diagenetic processes relevant to the early Earth and astrobiology.

Key questions:

- Which **morphological biosignatures** (filaments, tubular sheaths, twisted stalks) survive
  hydrothermal and low-grade metamorphic conditions?
- Can **pyrite** and other iron sulfides retain microbial morphologies, and how do biogenic
  pyrites differ from abiotic ones?
- How do organic matter, mineral templates and fluid chemistry steer **preservation versus
  degradation**?

:::

## Why it matters

Correctly identifying ancient fossils, and linking them to the environments they lived in,
lets us reconstruct past conditions on Earth and judge the habitability of other planets.
False positives (minerals that *look* biological) are among the biggest problems in the
search for early and extraterrestrial life. Experiments with known starting material are
one of the few ways to calibrate what we see.

## Approach

::: {.hv-grid}

::: {.hv-card .c-green}
[<i class="bi bi-1-circle"></i>]{.hv-card-icon}

#### Grow

Enrichments and pure cultures of sulfur-oxidizing and iron-oxidizing bacteria forming mats, sheaths and stalks.
:::

::: {.hv-card .c-yellow}
[<i class="bi bi-2-circle"></i>]{.hv-card-icon}

#### Mineralize

Encrust the biomass with iron (oxyhydr)oxides, iron sulfides and silica under anoxic, controlled chemistry.
:::

::: {.hv-card .c-orange}
[<i class="bi bi-3-circle"></i>]{.hv-card-icon}

#### Cook

Experimental diagenesis in hydrothermal and HPHT autoclaves, simulating burial and low-grade metamorphism.
:::

::: {.hv-card .c-purple}
[<i class="bi bi-4-circle"></i>]{.hv-card-icon}

#### Analyse

SEM-EDX, µRaman, µXRD, FTIR, SIMS, lipid biomarkers and synchrotron imaging to see what survived.
:::

:::

#### Filamentous sulfur mats under hydrothermal conditions

#### Iron-oxidizers as hidden sources of pyrite microfossils

#### Iron-rich stalactites and Mars

Geomicrobiology of iron-rich cave stalactites, and what it implies for the habitability of iron-rich deposits on Mars.
